summary: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.’s 2022 Form 10-K identifies the company, reporting period, incorporation, address, securities and exchanges, filing status, filer classifications, internal-control attestation, market value, outstanding shares, and incorporated proxy materials. Its contents outline business and risk disclosures; properties, legal and mine-safety matters; stock and market information; management analysis and market-risk disclosures; financial statements and notes; accounting, controls, governance, executive compensation, ownership, related-party matters, auditor fees, exhibits, schedules, and signatures.

title: Berkshire Hathaway Business and Workforce
summary: Berkshire Hathaway is a Delaware holding company headquartered in Omaha, with major insurance, rail, utility and energy businesses, plus diverse manufacturing, service, retail and other operations. Its businesses are managed decentrally; senior management oversees capital allocation, investments, executive selection and governance, while the Board ensures CEO succession and a code sets ethical and legal standards. At year-end 2022, Berkshire employed about 383,000 people worldwide; its subsidiaries set varied policies covering safety, compensation and benefits, wellness, training, career development, hiring, diversity and inclusion. U.S. workforce demographics are available on its website.

title: Insurance and Reinsurance Businesses

nodes.title: Insurance and Reinsurance Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s insurance and reinsurance operations, workforce, risk types, contract classifications, competition and underwriting principles are described, along with U.S., international and group-level regulatory frameworks, capital strength and ratings. The text explains TRIA terrorism coverage, eligibility, deductibles, reimbursement and limits; foreign regulatory variation, Berkshire’s international structure and Brexit response; and Alleghany’s acquisition and businesses. It outlines underwriting groups and profiles GEICO’s products, distribution, competition, market share and claims operations, plus Primary Group insurers’ coverages, markets and distribution.

nodes.title: GEICO
nodes.summary: The text describes GEICO’s headquarters, insurance subsidiaries, personal and specialty products, distribution and claims operations, competitors, market share and policy trends, pandemic and supply-chain effects, regulation, weather-related claims exposure, and emphasis on cost-efficient service and brand protection. It then outlines Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group’s independently managed insurers, their products, customers, locations, geographic reach, and distribution channels, including NICO Primary, BHHC, BH Specialty, RSUI, CapSpecialty, MedPro, USLI, GUARD, BH Direct, and MLMIC. Finally, it describes Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group’s global property, casualty, life, and health reinsurance operations, constituent groups and bases, and how underwriting volume varies with market conditions, pricing, coverage terms, and large transactions.

nodes.title: Property/casualty
nodes.summary: The text describes Berkshire’s insurance operations: NICO and General Re’s property/casualty reinsurance and specialty coverage, TransRe’s treaty and facultative business, General Re’s global life/health reinsurance, and BHLN’s life, variable-annuity risk, and periodic-payment annuity business. It explains retroactive reinsurance, its long-duration losses, investment rationale, and time-value-of-money pricing. It outlines insurance investments, concentrated equity holdings, float growth from $114 billion in 2017 to $164 billion in 2022, and float costs. Finally, it describes BNSF’s North American railroad, workforce, and smaller logistics business.

nodes.title: Insurance Reinsurance, Annuities and Investments
nodes.summary: The page describes TransRe’s property-casualty reinsurance and General Re and BHLN life and health businesses, including their markets, products and distribution. It explains NICO retroactive reinsurance, its coverage, long-tail claims, time-value pricing and expected underwriting losses offset by investment benefits; and BHLN periodic-payment annuities for structured settlements, with upfront premiums, long-term payments and expected accretion-related losses. It also summarizes Berkshire insurance investments, portfolio approach, float sources and growth from $114 billion in 2017 to $164 billion in 2022, and float costs in 2020–2022.

summary: Berkshire’s insurance and reinsurance businesses are described, including their underwriting principles, risks, competition, workforce, regulatory frameworks, capital strength, ratings, terrorism coverage and international operations, including Brexit and Alleghany. The section profiles GEICO and Primary Group insurers, their products, markets, distribution, claims and operating trends, and outlines global property-casualty, life and health reinsurance, retroactive reinsurance and periodic-payment annuities. It also covers insurance investments, concentrated holdings, float growth and cost, and BNSF’s railroad and logistics operations.

title: Railroad Business—Burlington Northern Santa Fe
summary: BNSF, headquartered in Fort Worth, operates a major North American railroad and a smaller logistics business, employing about 36,000 people, mostly union members. Its network serves U.S. regions, ports, Canada and Mexico through major routes, shortlines and carrier partnerships; 2022 freight revenues came from consumer, industrial, agricultural and coal products. Performance depends partly on economic conditions. Federal, state, local and Canadian regulators oversee rates, routes, service, construction, safety, health, hazardous materials and environmental matters, affecting costs and profitability. Environmental risks include pollution, hazardous-material transport and potentially strict cleanup liability on current or former industrial properties. Diesel produced about 80% of 2018 GHG emissions; BNSF targets a 30% reduction by 2030 through efficiency, renewable diesel and testing battery-electric and hydrogen locomotives. Competition comes from railroads, trucks, barges, ships and pipelines, with trucks and possible longer combination vehicles challenging time-sensitive freight; BNSF pursues efficiency amid intensifying rail competition, especially with Union Pacific in the West.

title: Utilities and Energy Businesses—Berkshire Hathaway Energy

nodes.title: General Matters
nodes.summary: Berkshire owns 92% of BHE, a 24,000-employee global energy company spanning regulated utilities, gas pipelines, international electricity networks, renewable power, LNG facilities, and U.S. real estate brokerage. Its U.S. utilities serve 5.2 million customers across several states, own about 29,500 MW of generation, sell power and gas at retail and wholesale, and face seasonal demand. Its pipeline businesses operate about 21,200 miles, storage facilities, and LNG assets, serving broad markets with seasonal variations. Other operations include electricity distribution in England, transmission in Alberta, about 6,000 MW of contracted independent generation—mostly renewable—and $7.3 billion in third-party wind tax-equity investments.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: U.S. utilities face broad federal, state and local oversight. FERC regulates wholesale electricity, transmission, reliability, utility holding companies, records, securities, hydro facilities and other matters, and may impose significant civil penalties; MEC is also subject to NRC oversight for its Quad Cities Nuclear Station ownership. Utilities generally have exclusive retail service territories and service obligations, though customer choice and self-generation are permitted in some areas. State commissions typically set cost-of-service retail rates, including a reasonable return, with bundled and transmission- or distribution-only options. The text also describes formula-based UK distribution charges and price-control periods; Alberta AUC oversight of AltaLink tariffs, rates, facilities and financing, alongside AESO system operation and planning; and FERC regulation of specified interstate gas pipelines, storage and LNG facilities, plus federal pipeline safety rules administered by DOT’s pipeline safety office.

nodes.title: Environmental Matters
nodes.summary: BHE faces extensive environmental laws covering air, climate, water, coal ash and other matters, with compliance costs and penalties. The text reviews emissions regulation and potential clean-energy standards; the Paris Agreement’s goals, U.S. withdrawal, reentry and 2030/2035 pledges; EPA power-plant rules, court decisions and planned replacement; and proposed methane rules. BHE’s emissions chiefly come from coal and gas generation. It reports $31.6 billion invested in renewable generation, 16 coal units retired, emissions down over 27% from 2005 by 2022, and plans for further investment and 16 more retirements by 2030 to target a 50% reduction.

nodes.title: Non-Energy Businesses
nodes.summary: HomeServices of America is a U.S. residential real estate brokerage offering traditional brokerage and integrated services, including mortgages, title and closing, insurance, warranties, relocation and other home-related services. It operates 55 brands across 33 states and D.C., with about 45,000 agents in nearly 930 offices. Its franchise network has about 300 franchisees, over 1,500 offices and nearly 51,000 agents, chiefly in the U.S.; for fees, it licenses two brands and provides training, consultation, advertising and related support. Revenue depends on home sales, typically stronger in the second and third quarters, and the business faces intense competition and general market conditions.

summary: Berkshire owns 92% of BHE, a global energy business spanning U.S. regulated utilities and gas pipelines, international electricity networks, renewable and contracted generation, LNG, and real estate brokerage. The section describes its customers, assets, seasonal markets, and operations; the extensive federal, state, UK and Alberta regulation governing rates, service, facilities, safety and reliability; and environmental requirements, emissions rules, renewable investment, coal retirements and reduction targets. It also covers HomeServices of America’s brokerage and integrated home services, franchise operations, scale, seasonal revenue, competition and market exposure.

title: Manufacturing Businesses

nodes.title: Industrial products
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses are grouped into industrial, building and consumer products and employed about 191,000 people in 2022. This excerpt details industrial businesses: Precision Castparts’ aerospace, power, alloy, casting, forging and fastener products, markets, pandemic recovery, competition, supply and environmental risks; Lubrizol’s specialty chemicals, segments, global operations, innovation, customers, disruptions, investment and regulatory risks; IMC’s carbide cutting tools, global sales, competition, tungsten supply and environmental practices; and Marmon’s diverse manufacturing and service groups, including railcars, tank containers, cranes and medical devices. Other businesses include agricultural systems maker CTB, pipeline drag-reduction provider LSPI, Scott Fetzer companies and Alleghany additions, including structural steel.

nodes.title: Building Products
nodes.summary: The text profiles Berkshire Hathaway’s building-products businesses: Clayton’s factory- and site-built homes, financing, sales channels, backlogs, acquisitions, input and labor pressures, interest-rate effects, and regulation; Shaw’s flooring, turf, and geosynthetics products, manufacturing, distribution, materials, and competition; Johns Manville’s insulation, roofing, and fiberglass products, facilities, materials, markets, seasonality, and environmental compliance; MiTek’s residential and commercial building products and steel supply; Benjamin Moore’s coatings, brands, retail and online channels, competition, raw-material constraints, and environmental commitments; and Acme’s brick, block, and distributed products, facilities, seasonal demand, raw-material supply, and emissions compliance.

nodes.title: Consumer Products
nodes.summary: The consumer products section covers Forest River’s RVs, trailers, buses and boats, its brands, dealer network, market position, competition and safety regulation; apparel and footwear businesses FOL, Garan, Fechheimer, BH Shoe Holdings and Brooks, including their products, brands, sourcing, distribution, raw materials and competition; and other businesses Duracell (batteries, global operations, market share and materials), Albecca (custom framing and related services), Richline (jewelry and specialty-market products), and Jazwares, a global toy company acquired in 2022.

summary: Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses are grouped into industrial, building and consumer products and employed about 191,000 people in 2022. The section profiles their major companies, products, operations, markets, brands, customers, sales and distribution, competition, acquisitions, and pandemic recovery. It also covers supply and labor constraints, input costs, investment and innovation, seasonality, interest-rate effects, and environmental, regulatory and product-safety risks across aerospace and industrial goods, chemicals, construction products, homes, flooring, apparel, footwear, batteries, framing, jewelry, toys, vehicles and other products.

title: Service and Retailing Businesses

nodes.title: Service Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s service businesses employed about 55,000 people in 2022 and span distribution, aviation, restaurants, media, logistics and related services. McLane distributes groceries, foodservice products and beverages nationwide, serving major retailers and restaurants through three divisions. FlightSafety provides aviation training and develops and sells simulators and training technology. NetJets offers private aviation, shared aircraft ownership, flight cards and management services under extensive aviation regulation. TTI distributes electronic components worldwide to diverse industries. Other businesses include XTRA trailer leasing; Dairy Queen restaurant franchising; Business Wire news distribution; CORT furniture rental and sales; WPLG television; Charter Brokerage logistics; and IPS project, engineering and consulting services.

nodes.title: Retailing Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s retailing businesses employed about 26,000 people in 2022 and span automotive, home furnishings, jewelry, confectionery, kitchenware, party goods and motorcycle products. BHA operates 106 franchises at 83 dealerships, plus collision centers, auctions and related businesses; revenue is concentrated in Arizona and Texas and a few brands. The text describes its competition, manufacturer and franchise agreements, and vehicle and insurance protection products. Home-furnishings retailers NFM, R.C. Willey, Jordan’s and Star are profiled by locations, facilities and market position. Other retailers include Borsheims, Helzberg, Ben Bridge, See’s, Pampered Chef, Oriental Trading and Louis, with their products, channels and geographic reach noted. Berkshire owned 38.6% of Pilot through 2022, then acquired control in January 2023. Pilot’s travel-center, fuel, wholesale and related operations, scale, competition, customer and supplier concentration, low-carbon fuels, planned EV and truck charging networks, and environmental obligations are summarized.

summary: Berkshire’s service businesses employed about 55,000 people in 2022 across food and electronics distribution, aviation training and private travel, logistics, restaurants, media, leasing, and engineering and consulting. Its retailing businesses employed about 26,000, spanning automotive dealerships and related services, home furnishings, jewelry, confectionery, kitchenware, party goods, and motorcycle products. The section profiles these operations, their markets, products, locations, competition, agreements, and customer and supplier concentration. It also covers Berkshire’s Pilot ownership transition, Pilot’s travel-center and fuel businesses, growth plans for lower-carbon fuels and charging networks, and environmental obligations.

title: Berkshire Risk Factors
key_items: General Business Risks Terrorist acts could hurt our operating businesses.
We are dependent on a few key people for our major investment and capital allocation decisions.
We need qualified personnel to manage and operate our various businesses.
summary: Berkshire identifies known and potential business risks, including terrorist attacks that may damage operations, people, or systems; increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks that could disrupt services, compromise information, cause financial and reputational harm, or limit access to capital and technology; reliance on Buffett and other key executives for major investment and capital decisions, partly mitigated by succession planning; and the need to recruit and retain qualified managers and employees across its decentralized businesses.

title: Key Business and Financial Risks
key_items: Investments are unusually concentrated in equity securities and fair values are subject to loss in value.
Competition and technology may erode our business franchises and result in lower earnings.
Unfavorable general economic conditions may significantly reduce our operating earnings and impair our ability to access capital markets at a reasonable cost.
Epidemics, pandemics or other similar outbreaks could hurt our operating businesses.
Regulatory changes may adversely impact our future operating results.
Climate change and the regulation of greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions may impact our businesses.
summary: The page outlines risks from concentrated equity investments and potential declines in value, competitive and technological pressures, economic downturns and restricted or costly capital-market access, and epidemics or pandemics. It also covers regulatory changes and privacy-compliance penalties, plus climate-related extreme weather, physical and insurance losses, and GHG policies that may raise costs or harm financial results.

title: Risks unique to our regulated businesses Our tolerance for risk in our insurance businesses may result in significant underwriting losses.
summary: The company’s willingness to assume unusually large insured risks could lead to major losses from natural or man-made catastrophes, despite underwriting controls intended to limit single-event exposure to $15 billion; unforeseen loss patterns or unenforceable policy exclusions could defeat mitigation and reduce earnings. Property and casualty claims may take decades to emerge and settle, making premiums and reserves inherently uncertain. Changing industry practices, laws, social conditions, and liability theories may expand coverage beyond underwriting intent, with full obligations unknown for years. Unpaid-loss estimates were $143 billion at year-end 2022, so even a small increase could materially lower earnings.

title: Changes in regulations and regulatory actions can adversely affect our operating results and our ability to allocate capital.
summary: The text explains how regulatory changes may constrain Berkshire’s insurance businesses, BNSF railroad, and BHE utilities and energy operations, affecting rates, investments, dividends, capital allocation, compliance costs, and financial results. It notes BNSF’s exposure to coal-policy shifts, hazardous-material incidents, and rail regulation, as well as major ongoing capital needs and debt-market risks for BNSF and BHE. It reports no unresolved staff comments, then describes BNSF’s network across 28 U.S. states and three Canadian provinces, its tracks, facilities, equipment, and approximately $2 billion in 2022 repair and maintenance expense.

title: Regulatory Risks, Properties, and BNSF Operations
summary: BHE’s regulated utilities and energy businesses face complex, changing rules that can constrain operations and harm financial results if regulations change or are not met. Railroad and utility operations require substantial capital investment; project failures may not be recoverable through customer rates, and debt-market disruptions may impair results, liquidity, or capital resources. Item 1B reports no unresolved staff comments. Item 2 introduces business properties. BNSF operates more than 32,500 route miles across 28 states and three Canadian provinces, owning over 23,000 miles and using trackage rights on over 9,000; its system totals over 50,000 miles of track. It maintains extensive rail infrastructure, facilities, equipment, and about 25 intermodal hubs, owns or leases roughly 7,500 locomotives and 68,000 freight cars, and spent about $2 billion on repairs and maintenance in 2022.

title: Utilities and Energy Businesses—Berkshire Hathaway Energy
summary: The text describes Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s electricity and natural-gas assets, supporting rights and debt encumbrances; lists generating technologies, subsidiaries, locations, capacity, and facilities under construction; and summarizes utility networks and gas pipelines, storage and LNG operations. It also outlines property types and owned/leased locations across Berkshire’s other business segments. Finally, it discusses routine and other litigation, which management does not expect to materially affect results or financial condition, and directs readers to Exhibit 95 for mine-safety disclosures.

title: Pipeline Systems, Properties, Legal Proceedings and Mine Safety
summary: Describes Northern Natural’s pipeline mileage, service areas and storage facilities, and Kern River’s pipeline route. Summarizes other business segments’ properties by business, country, location, facility type and owned/leased counts. Notes routine and other pending litigation, which Berkshire does not expect to materially affect its financial condition or results. Mine safety disclosures are provided in Exhibit 95 to the Form 10-K.

title: Executive Officers, Risks, Stock, Shareholders and Dividends
summary: Lists Berkshire’s five named executive officers, positions, ages and service-start years, and explains their terms of office. Cautions that forward-looking statements are uncertain and not guaranteed, identifying risks including investment and derivative losses, catastrophic events, disease outbreaks, legal or tax changes, and economic and market shifts. Reports that Class A and B shares trade on the NYSE as BRK.A and BRK.B; gives approximate record-holder counts and nominee-held shares as of February 13, 2023; and notes Berkshire has declared no cash dividend since 1967.

title: Share Repurchases and Stock Performance
summary: Berkshire’s repurchase program allows Class A and B buybacks when Buffett and Munger judge shares conservatively valued below intrinsic value, via market or private transactions. Fourth-quarter 2022 repurchases are tabulated by month and share class; the program has no share or dollar limit or expiration date, but buybacks cannot reduce cash, equivalents, and Treasury bills below $30 billion. A performance graph compares $100 invested in Berkshire from December 31, 2017, with the S&P 500 and Property–Casualty Insurance indices; index returns reinvest dividends, and the latter is used because Berkshire lacks a suitable peer group. Item 6 is reserved.

title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations Results of Operations
summary: Berkshire reports three-year after-tax earnings by business segment, including investment and derivative gains or losses and impairment charges. It describes its decentralized management, corporate oversight and reliance on segment disclosures, and notes uncertain effects from COVID-19, supply disruptions, inflationary costs and geopolitical conflict. Insurance underwriting results are explained for 2020–2022, including catastrophe losses, GEICO claims and premium changes, reinsurance trends, foreign exchange effects and pandemic impacts. Insurance investment income rose in 2022 due to higher dividends and interest rates; low rates had reduced income in 2020–2021.

title: Results of Operations (Continued)

nodes.title: Insurance—Underwriting
nodes.summary: The text reviews Berkshire’s 2020–2022 operating results: BNSF earnings were flat in 2022 after rising in 2021; utilities and energy, and manufacturing, service and retailing earnings increased, with results shaped by volumes, demand, prices, costs and supply-chain disruptions. It discusses volatile investment gains and losses, foreign-exchange gains/losses and impairment charges. Insurance underwriting is evaluated separately from investment income and gains; catastrophe losses, reserve estimates and currency movements affect results. It describes insurance groups, Alleghany’s acquisition, underwriting goals and retroactive-contract economics, then presents underwriting results and GEICO operations. GEICO’s 2022 underwriting loss reflected claims inflation and higher severity, following pandemic-related frequency declines and subsequent increases in driving.

nodes.title: GEICO
GEICO (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire describes its insurance and reinsurance businesses, the 2022 Alleghany acquisition, and its long-term underwriting goals, noting expected losses on certain retroactive reinsurance and annuity contracts. The text presents consolidated underwriting results and GEICO’s business, results, and drivers for 2020–2022. GEICO’s 2022 underwriting loss reflected inflation-driven claim severity and rising frequency; premium growth from rate increases was partly offset by fewer policies, while lower advertising and employee costs improved the expense ratio. It details coverage-level frequency and severity trends, prior-year reserve reductions, catastrophe losses, and the effects of the COVID-era Giveback program. For 2021 versus 2020, it explains premium growth, increased claims and catastrophe losses, reserve releases, and lower expenses. Approved rate increases led management to expect an underwriting profit in 2023.

nodes.title: Insurance—Underwriting (Continued) Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group comprises independently managed commercial insurers offering healthcare professional liability, workers’ compensation, auto, general liability, property and specialty coverage; its principal insurers include BH Specialty, BHHC, MedPro, GUARD, NICO Primary and USLI, with Alleghany’s RSUI and CapSpecialty included from October 19, 2022. Premiums written rose 16.1% in 2022 and 23.3% in 2021, driven by growth across insurers and, in 2022, Alleghany’s addition. The text provides three-year underwriting results and reports a 1.9-point increase in the 2022 loss ratio after a 4.1-point decline in 2021. Catastrophe losses, pandemic-related liabilities, prior-year reserve reductions, long-tail claim uncertainty and workers’ compensation and liability exposures are discussed. Underwriting expenses rose 21.1% in 2022 and 20.4% in 2021, reflecting earned-premium growth and business mix.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group
nodes.summary: BHRG provides global property/casualty, life/health, retroactive reinsurance and periodic-payment annuity coverage through named subsidiaries, including TransRe from October 19, 2022. The text reports premiums and pretax underwriting results by business line for 2020–2022, plus property/casualty results. In 2022, property/casualty premiums written rose 19.9%, driven by new business, higher rates and TransRe, partly offset by currency effects; 2021 growth reflected new business, participation, renewal pricing and favorable currency. Losses rose 7.4% in 2022; catastrophe losses, including major hurricanes, pandemic losses in 2020, and prior-year reserve revisions are detailed. Expense ratios fell in 2022 and 2021, reflecting business mix and currency effects; foreign-exchange gains on liabilities are also reported.

nodes.title: Property/casualty
nodes.summary: BHRG reports premiums and pre-tax underwriting results by business line, then explains 2020–2022 property/casualty reinsurance results. Written premiums rose in 2022 due to new business, higher rates and TransRe, while catastrophe losses, prior-year reserve changes, expense ratios and currency gains affected results; 2021 premium growth and catastrophe losses are also detailed. Life/health premiums and benefits declined in 2022, with currency, regional volume, pandemic claims and a nonrenewed contract explaining trends and prior-year earnings. Retroactive reinsurance losses reflect deferred-charge amortization, currency effects and claim estimates; unpaid losses and deferred charges declined. Periodic-payment annuity premiums fluctuated, with volume driven by rates, risk, settlements and competition.

nodes.title: Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: Life/health reinsurance results show premiums written fell 7.8% in 2022, mainly from foreign-exchange effects and lower Asia-Pacific volume; 2021 premiums rose excluding a nonrenewing 2020 U.S. health contract. Benefits declined in 2022 after pandemic-related mortality raised 2021 claims; 2020 earnings were also affected by COVID claims and revised Australian disability assumptions. Retroactive reinsurance losses mainly reflect deferred-charge amortization, alongside currency gains or losses and claim-estimate changes; year-end 2022 unpaid losses and deferred charges declined. Periodic payment annuity premiums fell in 2022 after rising in 2021; business volume is sensitive to pricing, interest rates, risk, settlement timing, and competition.

nodes.title: Periodic payment annuity
nodes.summary: The passage reviews Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group life/health, retroactive reinsurance, periodic payment annuity and variable annuity underwriting, plus insurance investment income. Life/health premiums fell in 2022, mainly from currency effects and lower Asia-Pacific volume; benefits declined from elevated 2021 pandemic claims, while 2020 results reflected COVID claims and Australian disability-liability assumptions. Retroactive losses mainly reflected deferred-charge amortization, partly offset by currency gains; unpaid losses and deferred charges declined. Periodic annuity premiums fell in 2022, with losses affected by discount accretion, contract termination and currency gains; future accounting changes will put life-contingent discount-rate effects in comprehensive income. Variable-annuity gains reflected interest rates and markets. Investment income rose in 2022, driven by dividends, higher interest rates and Alleghany assets; the company prioritizes liquidity and safety in short-term investments.

nodes.title: Insurance Underwriting and Investment Income
nodes.summary: Periodic-payment annuities generally incur underwriting losses from liability discount accretion and currency changes; results, key liability balances and discount rates, and the expected 2023 accounting change are described. Variable-annuity reinsurance gains or losses reflect markets, rates, currencies, and profit-margin amortization. The page reports insurance investment income by category and year, explains changes in dividend and interest income—including portfolio growth, rate increases, and Alleghany assets—and notes preferred-stock income eliminations and the priority placed on liquidity and safety over yield.

nodes.title: Insurance—Investment Income (Continued)
nodes.summary: Insurance float, derived from shareholder capital and net policy liabilities less related receivables and deferred costs, was $164 billion at year-end 2022 (including $14 billion from Alleghany), versus $147 billion in 2021 and $138 billion in 2020. Insurance operations recorded a $98 million pretax underwriting loss in 2022, with nominal float cost; underwriting gains made float cost negative in 2021 and 2020. The text reports insurance cash and investment totals for 2022 and 2021 and gives 2022 fixed-maturity investments by category, including amortized cost, unrealized gains or losses, and carrying value. U.S. government obligations were rated AA+/Aaa, and about 93% of foreign government obligations were rated AA or higher; these securities include national or provincial government obligations or guarantees.

nodes.title: Railroad
nodes.summary: BNSF’s 2022 and 2021 results include revenues, expenses, earnings, tax rates and freight volumes by business group. In 2022, revenue rose 11.9% as average revenue per car/unit increased, but lower volume and higher fuel and operating costs reduced pretax earnings 1.9%. The text explains revenue and volume trends for consumer, industrial, agricultural and coal freight; rising expenses and the operating ratio; and 2020–22 union negotiations, agreements and ratification. It also details 2021 versus 2020 growth in revenue, earnings and volumes, business-group drivers, and expense changes, including fuel, labor, services and productivity.

nodes.title: Utilities and Energy
nodes.summary: The text describes BHE’s ownership, regulated utilities, gas pipelines, international and renewable energy operations, and real estate businesses, noting rate regulation and reporting 2020–2022 earnings. It explains 2022 and 2021 earnings changes by business and their drivers, including utility margins, customer volumes, tax credits, acquisitions, weather, taxes, foreign exchange, and interest rates. It then reports manufacturing, service and retailing revenues and earnings, acquisition-accounting exclusions, 2020 impairment exclusions, and manufacturing revenue, pretax earnings, and margins by industrial, building, and consumer products.

Reviews Berkshire’s insurance operations, including GEICO, primary insurance, and reinsurance: underwriting results and drivers, premiums, claims, catastrophe losses, reserves, expenses, business lines, float, investments, and fixed-maturity holdings. It also covers BNSF railroad results, freight volumes, costs, and labor agreements; BHE’s regulated utilities, pipelines, energy and real estate businesses and earnings drivers; and manufacturing, service, and retailing revenues, earnings, and margins.

summary: Reviews Berkshire’s 2020–2022 operating results across BNSF, utilities and energy, manufacturing, services and retailing, covering earnings, revenues, margins, volumes, demand, prices, costs, supply disruptions and labor agreements. It discusses volatile investment and foreign-exchange gains and losses and impairment charges. Insurance coverage includes underwriting results and goals, premiums, claims, catastrophe losses, reserves, expenses, float, investments and fixed-maturity holdings; insurance groups, Alleghany’s acquisition and retroactive-contract economics; and GEICO’s business and underwriting drivers, including pandemic-era driving patterns, claims inflation and rising severity.

title: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing Results
summary: Presents 2020–2022 revenues, pre-tax earnings, year-over-year changes, taxes and noncontrolling interests, net earnings, effective tax rates, and pre-tax margins for the manufacturing, service and retailing businesses; notes Pilot Travel Centers’ planned inclusion beginning January 31, 2023. Explains excluded acquisition-accounting expenses and 2020 impairment charges. Introduces manufacturing’s industrial, building, and consumer products categories and their revenue and pre-tax earnings summary.

It is presented in Management’s Discussion and Analysis.

nodes.title: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing (Continued) Industrial products
Manufacturing, Service and Retailing (Continued) Industrial products (intro)
nodes.summary: The industrial products group comprises PCC aerospace and industrial metals, Lubrizol specialty chemicals, IMC metalworking tools, Marmon’s diverse manufacturing, service and leasing businesses, CTB agricultural equipment, Scott Fetzer, LiquidPower, and—since October 2022—W&W|AFCO Steel and other acquired manufacturers. In 2022, group revenue rose 9.4% and pretax earnings 8.8%, with margin slightly lower. PCC revenue grew on aerospace recovery, but earnings barely rose amid cost, supply, labor and pension pressures. Lubrizol revenue and earnings increased, aided by pricing and insurance recoveries, despite lower volumes, costs and maintenance constraints. Marmon revenue and earnings rose broadly, offset partly by weaker rail leasing and Russia-related losses. IMC revenue increased, while earnings fell due to margins, costs, currency and geopolitical effects. In 2021, group revenue rose 9.8%, earnings 19.0%, and margin improved. PCC revenue fell amid pandemic-related aircraft declines, but earnings rebounded with restructuring progress. Lubrizol revenue increased while earnings dropped due to fire losses, higher costs and winter storms. Marmon revenue and earnings rose with recovery, higher volumes and prices, partly offset by divestitures and weaker leasing. IMC revenue and earnings increased with improving demand, efficiencies and favorable currency effects.

nodes.title: Building products
nodes.summary: Building products include Clayton Homes and businesses in flooring, insulation, roofing, engineered products, masonry, paint, and construction systems. In 2022, group revenue rose 15.7% and pretax earnings 41.3%, aided by demand, prices, and sales, but rising U.S. interest rates slowed homebuilding late in the year; declines are expected. Clayton revenue and earnings grew, driven by home prices, unit sales, and financial services, though fourth-quarter sales and backlog fell, foreclosures rose, and 2023 results are expected to weaken. Other businesses’ revenue and earnings increased on pricing, demand, divestiture gains, and lower charges. In 2021, group revenue and earnings also rose amid strong demand and supply-chain inflation; Clayton grew, while other businesses faced input constraints and higher restructuring costs. Consumer products include leisure vehicles, apparel, footwear, batteries, framing, jewelry, and Jazwares toys. 2022 revenue increased 3.1% from Forest River growth and Jazwares, partly offset by apparel, footwear, and Duracell declines; fourth-quarter revenue excluding Jazwares fell as RV sales weakened. Other building-products businesses gained revenue from higher prices and volumes, while supply disruptions and restructuring and impairment charges reduced margins. The consumer-products group’s businesses are described, including Jazwares’ acquisition. summary: Berkshire reported strong liquidity and a $472.4 billion equity balance at year-end 2022, down $33.8 billion, amid a $22.8 billion shareholder net loss that included $53.4 billion in after-tax investment losses. Year-end holdings included $125.0 billion in cash and Treasury bills and $333.9 billion in specified securities; the company bought and sold equity securities, acquired Alleghany, and later acquired more of Pilot. nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group’s unpaid losses primarily arise from NICO, General Re and TransRe. At year-end 2022, non-retroactive unpaid losses and adjustment expenses totaled $50.6 billion gross and $48.3 billion net after $2.2 billion recoverables, comprising property and casualty case and IBNR liabilities. These liabilities mainly relate to traditional excess-of-loss and quota-share coverage; losses may require judgmental allocation across lines. Reinsurance loss data varies in detail and reliability, often lacks dependable IBNR estimates, and arrives more slowly than primary-insurance data, with additional delays for retrocessions. Berkshire checks contract compliance, can audit cedents’ records, and generally negotiates coverage disputes; unresolved disputes may go to arbitration, and none are expected to materially harm results or financial condition. Berkshire’s estimates exceeded cedent estimates by about $650 million for certain legacy workers’ compensation claims.

nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance estimates unpaid losses and IBNR using actuarial methods informed by historical and industry data, business and claims changes, inflation, legal conditions, and contract terms. nodes.title: Significant Accounting Policies and Practices
key_items: (a) Nature of operations and basis of consolidation
(b) Use of estimates in preparation of financial statements
(c) Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments in U.S. Treasury Bills
nodes.summary: Berkshire is a diversified holding company; its statements consolidate controlled subsidiaries and qualifying variable-interest entities, eliminate intercompany transactions, and may reclassify immaterial prior-year balances. GAAP financial reporting uses estimates, notably for insurance claims, reinsurance charges, fair values, and impairment; actual results may differ. COVID-19, supply-chain disruptions, geopolitical conflict, and inflation create uncertainty that could affect estimates and future results. Cash equivalents include demand deposits, money-market accounts, and investments with maturities of three months or less; short-term Treasury bills mature in over three months but under one year.

nodes.title: (d) Investments in fixed maturity securities
nodes.summary: Fixed maturity securities are classified as held-to-maturity at amortized cost, trading at fair value through earnings, or generally available-for-sale at fair value; cost-to-maturity differences are amortized using the interest method. Available-for-sale gains and losses are recognized on sale, while unrealized losses are assessed for intent to sell and credit impairment, with credit allowances charged to earnings and noncredit losses recorded in other comprehensive income. Equity securities are generally fair-valued through earnings. Equity-method investments apply when significant influence exists, generally presumed above 20%; carrying values reflect share of earnings, losses and other comprehensive income, less distributions, with certain additional losses possible. Loans are mainly manufactured-home loans, carried at amortized cost less expected-credit-loss allowances; related costs, fees and premiums or discounts adjust yield. Credit estimates consider payment performance, historical and current factors, forecasts, collateral and expected cash flows.

nodes.title: Accounting for Investment Securities
nodes.summary: Available-for-sale fixed maturity securities’ realized gains and losses use specific identification; unrealized losses are assessed for intent to sell and credit impairment, with credit allowances charged to earnings and noncredit losses recorded in other comprehensive income. Equity securities are generally measured at fair value, with changes in earnings. The equity method applies to investments with significant influence, generally presumed above 20% voting interest, in qualifying common-stock-like interests. Investments begin at cost and change for the investor’s share of earnings, losses, and comprehensive income; distributions reduce carrying value. Further losses may be recognized after the balance reaches zero when other investee investments are at risk.

nodes.title: (g) Loans and finance receivables
nodes.summary: Loans are mainly manufactured-home receivables, generally carried at amortized cost with expected-credit-loss allowances; estimates reflect loan performance, historical and forecast factors, and collateral. Policies specify delinquency, nonaccrual, foreclosure, interest recognition, and charge-offs. Other receivables include customer, insurance, and reinsurance balances, net of allowances, with losses estimated using history, forecasts, and counterparty credit enhancements. Derivatives are measured at fair value, with changes recorded in earnings or regulated accounts. Fair value uses market-participant assumptions and may require judgment. Inventories include manufactured goods and homes; costs use LIFO for about 30% and other methods otherwise, with non-LIFO items at lower cost or net realizable value.

nodes.title: Receivables, Derivatives, and Fair Value Policies
nodes.summary: Other receivables include customer, insurance, and reinsurance balances, reported net of estimated credit-loss allowances; expected losses reflect historical experience, economic forecasts, counterparty credit quality, offsets, and credit enhancements, with write-offs after collection efforts are exhausted. Derivatives are recorded at fair value, net of permitted master-agreement offsets; valuation changes go to earnings or, for regulated utilities when rate recovery is probable, regulatory assets or liabilities. Fair value reflects an orderly market-participant transaction, accounting for market conditions and liability credit risk, and requires judgment, so estimates may differ from realizable amounts.

nodes.title: (k) Inventories
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for inventories, property and equipment, leases, and goodwill. Inventories use LIFO for about 30% and FIFO or average cost otherwise, with non-LIFO inventory at lower of cost or net realizable value; it reports the LIFO replacement-cost excess for 2022 and 2021. Property and leased equipment are recorded at cost, with capitalization, repair, depreciation methods and useful-life ranges, disposal treatment, and impairment procedures described. Lease accounting covers right-of-use assets, liabilities, payments, terms, options, rates, and practical expedients. Goodwill’s definition, annual impairment testing, valuation methods, and impairment recognition are explained.

nodes.title: Property, Equipment, and Lease Accounting
key_items: (l) Property, plant and equipment and equipment held for lease
nodes.summary: Property and leased equipment are recorded at cost, including qualifying construction costs and, for regulated facilities, an allowance for funds used during construction; routine maintenance is expensed. Depreciation methods, asset life ranges, retirement accounting, and disposal gains or losses vary by business and asset type. Assets are tested for impairment when triggered, with losses generally measured against fair value and regulatory effects considered for regulated businesses. Leases from others create right-of-use assets and liabilities for fixed and index- or rate-based payments; terms generally exclude optional periods unless exercise is reasonably certain. Incremental borrowing rates are generally used, right-of-use assets are reviewed for impairment, and certain component-separation and short-term lease exemptions are applied.

nodes.title: (n) Goodwill and other intangible assets
nodes.summary: Goodwill is the excess of a business’s acquisition price over the fair value of its identified net assets and is tested for impairment at least annually. Reporting-unit fair value may be estimated using market quotations, asset and liability values, discounted earnings or cash flows, and earnings multiples; any carrying-value excess over fair value, limited to goodwill, is recognized as an impairment loss. Indefinite-lived intangible assets are tested annually and when impairment indicators arise, with significant judgment required. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized according to benefit consumption or straight-line over useful lives and reviewed for impairment when indicators suggest their carrying amounts may not be recoverable.

nodes.title: (o) Revenue recognition
nodes.summary: The text describes revenue recognition for insurance and reinsurance premiums, product sales, freight, energy, other services, and leases, including timing, performance obligations, pricing, incentives, taxes, and refunds. It explains estimates and accounting for unpaid insurance losses and recoveries; deferred charges and amortization for retroactive reinsurance; and capitalization, amortization, recoverability, and reported balances of insurance acquisition costs.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition and Insurance Loss Accounting
nodes.summary: Energy revenue is recognized as energy or services are delivered, based on regulated tariffs or contracts; revenue includes billed and unbilled amounts, and estimated refunds are accrued when preliminary rates may change. Other service revenue is recognized over time or when services are provided, while lease revenue is recognized over the lease term or by usage. Insurance liabilities for incurred losses are estimated undiscounted using reported claims, case estimates and incurred-but-unreported losses; earnings reflect claims and liability changes net of reinsurance recoveries, though ceding insurers retain policyholder obligations. Retroactive reinsurance also creates deferred charge assets for excess estimated claims over premiums, amortized using the interest method; estimate changes are applied retrospectively and recognized in insurance losses.

nodes.title: (r) Insurance policy acquisition costs
nodes.summary: The text describes policies for insurance acquisition costs, future life, annuity, and health benefit liabilities, regulated utility accounting, foreign currency translation and transaction gains or losses, and income taxes. It explains capitalization and amortization of acquisition costs and their reported balances; assumptions, discounting, and earnings effects for benefit liabilities; deferral and reassessment of regulatory assets and liabilities; currency translation in equity versus transaction effects in earnings; and current and deferred taxes, valuation allowances, and uncertain tax positions.

nodes.title: Insurance, Regulated Operations, and Foreign Currency Policies
key_items: (s) Life, annuity and health insurance benefits
nodes.summary: The page explains how life, annuity, and health insurance liabilities are estimated from expected benefits, expenses, premiums, and assumptions for investment yields, mortality, morbidity, and lapses; assumptions are generally set at contract inception, with changes recorded in earnings, and annuity liabilities are discounted using inception-date rates. Regulated energy businesses defer recoverable costs and accrued customer refunds as regulatory assets and liabilities, reassess their probable rate recovery, and recognize amounts no longer probable in earnings, other comprehensive income, or customer refunds. Foreign subsidiaries’ statements are translated at average rates for revenues and expenses and period-end rates for assets and liabilities, with translation effects in accumulated other comprehensive income; transaction and remeasurement gains or losses enter earnings.

nodes.title: (v) Income taxes
nodes.summary: Berkshire describes its income tax accounting: consolidated U.S. federal and other jurisdictional returns, current and deferred taxes, tax-rate changes, valuation allowances, and uncertain tax positions, including related interest and penalties. It adopted ASC 326 in 2020, recording a $388 million after-tax retained-earnings charge. It adopted ASU 2018-12 in 2023 using the modified retrospective method; the standard changes insurance liability assumptions and reporting, with specified historical equity effects and an immaterial net-earnings impact. The text also states Berkshire’s acquisition criteria and reports its October 2022 purchase of Alleghany for about $11.5 billion, describing its insurance, reinsurance, and non-financial businesses.

nodes.title: Adoption of Accounting Pronouncements
key_items: (x) New accounting pronouncements to be adopted subsequent to December 31, 2022
nodes.summary: The page describes adoption of ASC 326 in 2020, which measures expected credit losses on amortized-cost assets and resulted in a $388 million after-tax retained-earnings charge. It also explains ASU 2018-12’s revised assumptions, measurement, presentation, disclosure, and retrospective requirements for long-duration insurance contracts, its adoption on January 1, 2023 using the modified retrospective method, and resulting equity effects: reductions of $6.4 billion at 2020 year-end and $4.6 billion at 2021 year-end, followed by an expected $1.0 billion increase at 2022 year-end. Effects primarily reflect discount-rate changes; 2021 and 2022 earnings impacts are immaterial.

nodes.title: (2) Significant business acquisitions
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s acquisition strategy targets businesses with consistent earnings, strong equity returns, and capable, honest management; acquired results enter consolidated statements from acquisition dates. In 2022, Berkshire bought all Alleghany shares for about $11.5 billion. Preliminary acquisition accounting lists assets, liabilities, and net assets, with some valuations still provisional. Alleghany contributed about $2.4 billion in revenue and $216 million in earnings in 2022; pro forma 2021–22 revenues, shareholder earnings, and per-share results are provided. In 2020, BHE bought Dominion businesses for about $2.5 billion, including pipeline and storage operations and a 25% economic interest in Cove Point. Because BHE directs Cove Point’s key activities and bears potentially significant risks and benefits, it consolidates the VIE.

nodes.title: (3) Investments in fixed maturity securities
nodes.summary: The text presents fixed-maturity investment balances by security type for 2022 and 2021, showing amortized cost, unrealized gains and losses, and fair value. It notes that about $9.1 billion of 2022 U.S. Treasury holdings mature in 2023–2024; foreign government holdings include national and provincial securities and unconditional guarantees, with about 93% rated AA or higher. It also gives 2022 amortized cost and fair value by contractual maturity, noting actual maturities may differ because of issuer prepayment rights.

nodes.title: (4) Investments in equity securities
nodes.summary: Equity securities by industry are reported at cost, unrealized gains and fair value for 2022 and 2021. Fair value totaled $308.8 billion in 2022, with about 75% concentrated in five named companies, and $350.7 billion in 2021, with about 73% in four named companies. After its voting interest in Occidental exceeded 20% in August 2022, the company applied the equity method to its common stock, while keeping preferred stock and warrants at fair value. Occidental preferred stock has $10 billion liquidation value, 8% dividends and specified redemption terms; warrants cover up to 83.86 million shares at $59.62 and expire one year after preferred-stock redemption. Despite a 20.4% stake in American Express, voting arrangements and Federal Reserve passivity commitments limit significant influence, so its shares remain at fair value rather than under the equity method.

nodes.title: (5) Equity method investments
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s equity-method investments include 26.6% of Kraft Heinz and, as of August 4, 2022, 21.4% of Occidental (excluding potential warrant exercise). The text describes both companies and notes Occidental results are recorded one quarter late. It reports 2022 and 2021 carrying and fair values, plus investment earnings and distributions for 2020–2022. Summarized financial data for Kraft Heinz and Occidental is provided. Other investments include 38.6% of Pilot (increased to 80% in January 2023, ending equity-method accounting) and 50% of Berkadia; Berkadia’s business, borrowing support, and Jefferies’ indemnity obligation are outlined.

nodes.title: (6) Investment and derivative contract gains (losses)
nodes.summary: The text reports investment and derivative contract gains/losses for 2020–2022, including equity securities, fixed-maturity securities, and derivatives. Equity results include fair-value changes on securities still held and gains/losses on sales; equity-sale proceeds were $33.7 billion, $15.8 billion, and $38.8 billion, while taxable gains were $769 million, $3.6 billion, and $6.2 billion, respectively. Derivative results came from equity-index put options; three contracts were open at year-end 2022, one later expired, and future loss exposure was insignificant.

nodes.title: (7) Loans and finance receivables
nodes.summary: The notes report loans and finance receivables, their credit-loss allowances and discounts, and allowance rollforwards for 2020–2022. They describe loan types, impairment evaluation, payment status, and performing/non-performing home loans by origination year, plus commercial loan balances and Seritage exposure. Other receivables are detailed by business category, with credit-loss provisions and charge-offs. The text also lists inventory categories and property, plant and equipment by asset type, accumulated depreciation, and year-end balances for 2021 and 2022.

nodes.title: Other Receivables and Inventories
nodes.summary: The page presents December 31, 2022 and 2021 other receivables, broken down between insurance and other and railroad, utilities and energy categories, including credit-loss allowances. It reports provisions for credit losses for 2022–2020 and net charge-offs for those years. It also lists inventory categories: raw materials, work in process and other, finished manufactured goods, and goods acquired for resale.

nodes.title: (10) Property, plant and equipment
nodes.summary: The notes present December 31, 2022 and 2021 property, plant and equipment balances, in millions, for insurance and other businesses; railroad; and utilities and energy. They list asset categories, accumulated depreciation, and net book values, and note that regulated utility and pipeline subsidiaries own the utility systems and interstate pipeline assets. The text also introduces depreciation expense for the three years ended December 31, 2022, for insurance and other, and railroad, utilities and energy.

nodes.title: (11) Equipment held for lease
nodes.summary: Equipment held for lease includes railcars, aircraft, and other items such as trailers, tank containers, cranes, storage units, and furniture. The text reports equipment categories and carrying amounts net of accumulated depreciation for 2022 and 2021, plus depreciation expense of $1,209 million in 2022, $1,158 million in 2021, and $1,200 million in 2020. Fixed and variable lease revenues are given for 2020–2022, and future operating lease receipts at December 31, 2022 total $10,389 million, scheduled from 2023 through thereafter.

nodes.title: (12) Leases
nodes.summary: The note describes operating leases, primarily for buildings, offices and facilities, and where right-of-use assets and lease liabilities are reported. At December 31, 2022 versus 2021, assets were $4,975 million versus $5,091 million and liabilities $4,939 million versus $4,991 million; average remaining terms were 7.0 and 7.2 years, with discount rates of 3.7% and 3.5%. It presents future payments by year, totaling $5,651 million and $5,731 million, less interest of $712 million and $740 million, respectively. Lease costs for 2022, 2021 and 2020 include operating, short-term and variable costs, sublease income, and total costs of $1,799 million, $1,793 million and $1,776 million.

nodes.title: (13) Goodwill and other intangible assets
nodes.summary: The note reconciles goodwill for 2022 and 2021: balances rose from $73.7 billion to $78.1 billion in 2022, mainly from $4.7 billion of acquisitions, and ended 2021 at $73.9 billion; both year-end balances are net of $11.0 billion in accumulated impairments. It summarizes gross, accumulated amortization and net carrying values of other intangible assets by category for both years. Amortization expense was $1.233 billion in 2022, $1.252 billion in 2021 and $1.277 billion in 2020; estimates for 2023–2027 are $1.253 billion, $1.128 billion, $1.081 billion, $1.000 billion and $877 million. Indefinite-lived intangibles were $18.3 billion in 2022 and $18.5 billion in 2021, mainly customer relationships and trademarks/trade names.

nodes.title: (14) Supplemental cash flow information
nodes.summary: Supplemental cash flow information for 2022, 2021, and 2020 (in millions) includes cash paid for income taxes and interest, with interest divided between insurance and other, and railroad, utilities, and energy. It also reports adjustments to operating cash flows for foreign currency gains or losses, goodwill and intangible-asset impairments, and other items, plus noncash investing and financing activities: acquisition-related liabilities assumed and operating lease liabilities arising from new right-of-use assets.

nodes.title: (15) Dividend restrictions – Insurance subsidiaries
nodes.summary: Insurance subsidiaries’ dividends are regulated; without prior approval, principal subsidiaries could pay about $35 billion in ordinary dividends in 2023. Securities and short-term investments deposited with U.S. state authorities totaled $4.9 billion at year-end 2022, versus $6.4 billion in 2021. U.S. subsidiaries’ statutory policyholder surplus was $272 billion and $301 billion, respectively, differing from GAAP because certain items—including reinsurance charges, acquisition costs, unrealized investment gains and related taxes, goodwill, and non-insurance entities—are treated differently or excluded.

nodes.title: (16) Unpaid losses and loss adjustment expenses
nodes.summary: The passage reconciles 2020–2022 claim liabilities, including incurred and paid losses, reinsurance recoverables, foreign currency effects, and Alleghany’s acquired liabilities. It discusses catastrophe losses, rising private-auto claim frequency and severity, and prior-year reserve releases by year and business line. Environmental, asbestos and latent-injury liabilities were about $2.1 billion in 2022 and 2021, with additional losses not reliably estimable. It also reconciles 2022 liabilities across GEICO, BH Primary and BHRG, and explains GEICO’s actuarial reserving methods, including average, case, case-development and IBNR estimates.

Presents 2020–2022 financing cash flows, foreign-exchange effects, changes in cash and restricted cash, annual balances, and the year-end breakdown by business group. It then covers Berkshire’s accounting policies and financial-statement estimates; cash, investments, receivables, loans, derivatives, inventory, property, leases, goodwill, revenue, insurance liabilities, regulated operations, currency, taxes, and acquisitions. Notes provide investment and acquisition details, credit-loss and property schedules, lease and intangible balances, cash-flow information, insurance dividend restrictions, and unpaid-loss reconciliations and reserving methods.

nodes.title: GEICO
nodes.summary: The notes report prior-year reserve reductions for 2020–2022 by primary insurance and reinsurance, describe environmental, asbestos and latent-injury liabilities and estimation uncertainty, and introduce a reconciliation of GEICO, BH Primary and BHRG claim liabilities. They explain GEICO’s actuarial methods and provide accident-year incurred and paid loss development, unpaid reserves, IBNR and claim counts for auto physical damage and liability. BH Primary disclosures describe methods and accident-year development for medical professional liability and workers’ compensation/other casualty, including Alleghany’s retrospective inclusion.

nodes.title: BHRG
BHRG (intro)
nodes.summary: The notes explain BHRG’s methods for estimating claims liabilities, including loss-development, Bornhuetter-Ferguson, frequency/severity, and ground-up techniques; reliance on cedent-reported losses, case reserves, and IBNR; and the treatment of catastrophe claims, inconsistent claim counts, and allocations between property and casualty. They present accident-year incurred and cumulative paid losses and ALAE, IBNR/case-development and net unpaid liabilities for property and casualty through 2022, including Alleghany retrospectively. Unaudited supplemental information also reports average annual net loss payout percentages by age for several insurance lines.

nodes.title: (17) Retroactive reinsurance contracts
nodes.summary: The text explains retroactive reinsurance coverage for losses from events before contract inception, including claim-payment terms, and presents 2020–2022 reconciliations of claim liabilities, incurred and paid losses, foreign currency effects, and earnings impacts. It describes contract-inception-based loss classifications, deferred charge amortization and balances, and AIG contract payments and unpaid liabilities. It outlines methods for estimating and periodically revising long-tail liabilities, including environmental, asbestos, and latent-injury exposures, aggregate limits, monitoring of legal and claims developments, and uncertainty that changing conditions could materially increase liabilities, which cannot be reliably quantified.

nodes.title: (18) Notes payable and other borrowings
nodes.summary: Note 18 summarizes 2022 and 2021 carrying values, interest rates, and maturities for insurance/other and railroad, utilities, and energy borrowings. It describes Berkshire and BHFC note issuances, repayments and upcoming maturities; BHFC’s financing purpose and Berkshire guarantees of BHFC and other subsidiary debt; foreign-currency note balances and exchange-rate gains and losses; and BHE and BNSF debt, issuances, security, covenants, and Berkshire’s lack of guarantees for their debt. It also reports covenant compliance, unused credit and commercial-paper capacity, and introduces expected principal repayments for the next five years.

nodes.title: (19) Income taxes
nodes.summary: The note presents income-tax-related figures, including scheduled future tax amounts, balance-sheet tax liabilities, and deferred tax assets and liabilities by category for 2021–2022. It explains the treatment of undistributed foreign earnings, reports current and deferred tax expense or benefit and reconciles effective taxes to statutory rates for 2020–2022, including tax credits. It also summarizes IRS and other jurisdiction audits, settlements, potential 2023 resolutions, and unrecognized tax benefits and expectations.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements at December 31, 2022
nodes.summary: Note 20 summarizes financial assets and liabilities at December 31, 2022 and 2021, presenting fair values by hierarchy in millions. It notes that carrying values of cash and cash equivalents, U.S. Treasury Bills, other receivables, accounts payable, accruals and other liabilities approximate fair value. The 2022 listing covers fixed-maturity securities by category, equity investments including Kraft Heinz and Occidental stock, loans and finance receivables, derivative assets and liabilities, and notes payable and other borrowings.

nodes.title: December 31, 2021
nodes.summary: Presents carrying and fair values of financial instruments at December 31, 2021, broken down by Level 1–3 inputs, including fixed-maturity and equity investments, loans, derivatives, and borrowings; notes derivative balance-sheet locations. Defines the three fair-value hierarchy levels and valuation approaches. Reconciles recurring Level 3 balances for 2020–2022, including equity investments and equity-index put liabilities, and reports 2022 Level 3 valuations for preferred stock and warrants, their techniques and assumptions, and restrictions affecting valuation and hedging.

nodes.title: (21) Common stock
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s 2019–2022 common-stock table reports issued, treasury and outstanding Class A and Class B shares, including conversions and repurchases; 1 million preferred shares are authorized but none issued. Class A has one vote and converts into 1,500 Class B shares; Class B has 1/1,500 of Class A’s dividend and distribution rights and 1/10,000 of its voting rights. The classes generally vote together, and Class B cannot convert to Class A. The text gives equivalent shares outstanding for 2021 and 2022 and explains equivalent-share earnings-per-share calculations. Repurchases are permitted when the Chair and CEO and Vice Chair judge the price below conservatively estimated intrinsic value, without a share limit or end date, provided cash, equivalents and Treasury bills remain at least $30 billion; Berkshire is not obligated to repurchase.

nodes.title: (22) Revenues from contracts with customers
nodes.summary: Explains revenue recognition when customers obtain control and summarizes 2020–2022 customer-contract revenue by segment and source, distinguishing other revenue not covered by GAAP customer-contract rules. Reports the transaction prices and expected fulfillment timing for significant remaining performance obligations over one year. Describes defined-benefit pension plans, benefit and contribution policies, pension expense components for 2020–2022, projected benefit obligations and funding arrangements, and 2021–2022 changes in pension obligations and assets and year-end funded status for BHE, other plans, and totals.

nodes.title: Revenue Obligations and Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Reports the timing of satisfaction for remaining performance obligations from electricity, natural gas, and other contracts. Describes defined benefit pension plans, benefit and funding arrangements, unfunded obligations, and regulated cost recovery; presents three years of pension expense and two years of pension obligation and asset reconciliations, including contributions, benefits, returns, actuarial changes, and funded status for BHE, other plans, and totals.

nodes.title: Plan assets
nodes.summary: Reports remaining performance obligations for customer contracts over one year, split by electricity and gas versus other sales and services and by expected fulfillment within or beyond 12 months. Describes defined-benefit pension plans, expense for 2020–2022, obligation and asset reconciliations, funded status, PBO and ABO amounts, underfunded plans, actuarial assumptions, expected benefit payments and 2023 contributions. Details plan-asset fair values by investment category and valuation level, investment objectives, pension-related other comprehensive income changes, and defined-contribution plans and expenses.

nodes.title: (24) Accumulated other comprehensive income
nodes.summary: Reports, in millions, annual after-tax changes in Berkshire Hathaway shareholders’ accumulated other comprehensive income for 2020–2022, with opening and closing balances and other comprehensive income and reclassifications into net earnings for unrealized investment gains/losses, foreign-currency translation, defined-benefit pension plans, other items, and the total.

nodes.title: (25) Business segment data
nodes.summary: The notes explain Berkshire’s segment-reporting approach, including grouping businesses by similar activities and reconciling segment results to consolidated statements. They identify insurance segments (GEICO, Primary Group, Reinsurance Group), BNSF, BHE, manufacturing, McLane, and service and retailing, with their business activities. Tables present three years of segment revenues and pretax earnings, plus reconciliation items such as investment and derivative gains or losses, unallocated interest, equity-method results, impairments, corporate items, eliminations, income taxes, and interest expense.

nodes.summary: Presents three years of consolidated business-segment data (in millions), including revenues, earnings or losses before income taxes, income tax expense or benefit, and interest expense. Operating businesses are broken down into insurance underwriting groups, insurance investment income and total insurance, BNSF, BHE, manufacturing, McLane, and service and retailing. Reconciliation items include investment and derivative gains or losses, unallocated interest expense, equity-method investments, goodwill and intangible-asset impairments, and corporate, eliminations, and other.

nodes.summary: The notes present three-year business-segment financial data, including revenues, pretax earnings or losses, income taxes, interest expense, capital expenditures, depreciation, goodwill, and identifiable assets for insurance and other operating businesses, plus reconciliations to consolidated totals. They also summarize property/casualty and life/health premiums written and earned by direct, assumed, and ceded categories, and premiums written by geographic region.

nodes.title: Business Segment Capital Expenditures and Depreciation
nodes.summary: Continued business segment data reports capital expenditures and depreciation of tangible assets for 2020–2022 across Berkshire Hathaway’s operating businesses: Insurance, BNSF, BHE, Manufacturing, McLane, and Service and retailing. Totals are provided for capital expenditures.

nodes.title: Reconciliation to consolidated amount
nodes.summary: The text presents 2020–2022 reconciliations of corporate and other goodwill and identifiable assets, plus insurance premiums written and earned by property/casualty and life/health segments, and written premiums by geographic region. It also reports consolidated sales, service and leasing revenues and their U.S. share, railroad, utilities and energy revenues and their U.S. share, and the geographic distribution of net property, plant, equipment and leased equipment at year-end 2022.

nodes.title: (26) Contingencies and Commitments
nodes.summary: The company describes routine insurance- and other business-related litigation, including possible punitive damages, and does not expect pending cases to materially affect its financial condition or results. Future ordinary-course purchase commitments total estimated payments of $12 billion in 2023, $5 billion in 2024, $3 billion in 2025, $2 billion each in 2026 and 2027, and $18 billion thereafter. Berkshire acquired control of Pilot in January 2023 after previously holding 38.6%; it will consolidate Pilot, remeasure its prior stake and recognize any gain, with acquisition disclosures deferred until the March 2023 interim report. Future buyouts of subsidiary noncontrolling interests are possible and depend on owners’ actions and interest values. In June 2022, BHE bought Gregory Abel’s shares for $870 million, and Berkshire recorded a $362 million capital charge.

title: CONSENT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM
summary: Deloitte & Touche consents to incorporating its February 25, 2023 reports on Berkshire Hathaway’s 2022 consolidated financial statements, schedule, and internal-control effectiveness into specified Form S-3 and S-8 registrations. CEO Warren Buffett and CFO Marc Hamburg certify that they reviewed the 2022 Form 10-K, that its disclosures and financial information are fairly presented, and describe their responsibilities for disclosure and financial controls, evaluations, and reporting deficiencies, weaknesses, changes, or relevant fraud. Both also certify under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 that the report complies with securities-law requirements and fairly presents the company’s financial condition and results.

title: MINE SAFETY VIOLATIONS AND OTHER LEGAL MATTER DISCLOSURES PURSUANT TO SECTION 1503(a) OF THE DODD-FRANK WALL STREET REFORM AND CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT
summary: The disclosure reports 2022 MSHA safety violations and legal matters at PacifiCorp coal mines and Acme Brick clay, shale, and limestone facilities. It explains inspections, appealability of reported citations and penalties, exclusion of inactive sites without events, and no Section 104(e) pattern-of-violations notices. A facility-by-facility table lists Section 104 significant-and-substantial citations, 104(b) orders, 104(d) citations/orders, 110(b)(2) violations, 107(a) imminent-danger orders, proposed assessments, fatalities, and legal actions; footnotes define these categories and note one labor complaint.
